context: A guide talking at the start of a backstage tour of a theatre

cues.t: Part 2. You will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at the start of a backstage tour of a theatre. First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Royal Crescent Theatre. I'm Owen, and for the next hour I'll be showing you the parts of the building that audiences never normally see.

Let me start with a little history. A lot of people in the town remember this building as a cinema, and it was one, from the 1930s until the late 1960s. But that's not what it was built for. When it opened in 1891, it was a concert hall, mainly for orchestras and choirs. It only became a theatre in 1974, after a long campaign by local people.

Now, a few rules. As we go round, you'll see a lot of costumes hanging on rails. Please don't touch them. That's not because they're valuable; in fact, many of them are quite cheap copies of historical clothes. It's because they've been checked and arranged for tonight's performance, and if anything goes missing, an actor could end up on stage without a vital piece of costume.

When we reach the stage itself, you'll notice something unusual about it. It slopes gently down towards the audience, which was quite common in older theatres, because it helps people at the back to see the actors' feet. There used to be a section in the middle that could turn round, but that was taken out years ago. And it isn't the biggest stage in the region, by the way. That's at the new arts centre in Kingsford.

People are often surprised by how many staff are needed. During a typical show, there are about thirty people working backstage: stage managers, technicians, dressers and so on. If you add the box office, the bar and the ushers, it's nearer forty-five, but they're front of house, not backstage.

And finally, at the end of the tour, everyone will receive a free poster from one of our past productions. Programmes for tonight's show are on sale in the foyer if you'd like one, but I'm afraid we don't offer discounts on tickets for tour groups.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
Right. Could you all look at the plan in your leaflet? We're standing just inside the stage door, on the west side of the building, which is where the actors and staff come in.

As you come in through the stage door and walk along the corridor, the first door on your left is the green room. That's where actors wait and relax when they're not needed on stage. Despite the name, it isn't green. The room opposite, on the right, is the stage manager's office.

The wardrobe department, where all the costumes are made and repaired, is directly behind the stage, in the middle of the back wall. It's in a good position, because costumes can be taken straight from there to either side of the stage.

The scenery workshop is the large room in the north-east corner of the building. It has very wide doors that open onto the side of the stage, so that even large pieces of scenery can be moved straight on. Don't confuse it with the store room in the opposite corner, the north-west, where furniture and props are kept.

Next, the rehearsal room. You might expect it to be close to the stage, but there wasn't enough space there. So it's on the east side of the building, next to the auditorium. It's the same size as the stage, so actors can practise their movements exactly.

And lastly, the lighting control room. Everything is controlled from there during a performance: the lights, the sound and the special effects. It's at the very back of the auditorium, behind the last row of seats, so the operators can see the stage exactly as the audience do.
Right, if you'd like to follow me, we'll start with the green room.
That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
